messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: Empirical Bayes
parts:
Hi,

I am working on PK modeling and came up on software called BestDose and PMetrics which are not using parametric model for each individual PK parameters (as opposed to Torsten and other stan based PK packages). After some research I found that software is based on nonparametric maximum likelihood method (NLME) to determine distribution of individual PK parameters.The method can be viewed as empirical Bayes method to estimate the conditional probability of individual PK parameters given the data. I also found that empirical Bayes "may be viewed as an approximation to a fully Bayesian treatment of a hierarchical model wherein the parameters at the highest level of the hierarchy are set to their most likely values, instead of being integrated out". By perusing stan user group postings I found that empirical Bayes may be emulated in stan by using weakly informative priors. It looks like NLME should be more effective than using weakly informative prior. I am trying to build a coherent picture about the applicability of fully Bayesian hierarchical and empirical Bayes approaches to PKPD modeling - what are benefits, disadvantages, what classes of problems are solved better/faster with one versus another, possible biases etc. Can somebody help? Are the any publications which compare two approaches?

Thanks in advance,
Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Empirical Bayes
parts:
There's no way to do "empirical Bayes" in Stan (quotes for Andrew's
benefit---it's no more empirical than full Bayes). You need to marginalize
out the low level parameters in order to maximize the high-level parameters
(or hack with cross-validation as is popular in machine learning).

We are working on adding max marginal likelihood (MML), which will let you
optimize the higher-level parameters. NONMEM uses MML if you want
a comparison in the PK/PD world.

You're better off using full Bayes. Empirical Bayes underestimates any
uncertainty having to do with high-level parameters by fixing them to
a single value. Thus it tends to produce uncalibrated results that
underestimate uncertainty in predictions. I just wrote a post on
Andrew's blog about why full Bayes is always calibrated (in expectation).

http://andrewgelman.com/2017/04/12/bayesian-posteriors-calibrated/

and Andrew's blogged on it previously:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/12/06/yes-checking-calibration-of-probability-forecasts-is-part-of-bayesian-statistics/

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Empirical Bayes
parts:
Hi, weakly informative priors are often ok; in other settings including some PK models, it's helpful to use strongly informative priors to better regularize the solution.  As Bob said in his reply, there's no real advantage to marginal likelihood; we'd rather just use full Bayes.  There are some problems where full Bayes is slow and marginal likelihood is faster, but except for that speed issue that sometimes arises, full Bayes should do better.
A
